questions.stem: A medication that would be acceptable to a patient who refuses all products derived from human plasma is

opts.why: Prothrombinex is a human-plasma-derived prothrombin complex concentrate.
Recombinant activated factor VII (NovoSeven RT) is produced by recombinant expression, not from donor plasma.
Standard fibrinogen concentrate is fractionated from donor human plasma.
Human albumin is purified from donor plasma.
Anti-D immunoglobulin is produced from donated human plasma.

questions.expl: NZ Blood identifies NovoSeven RT as recombinant (not derived from donor blood); Prothrombinex, fibrinogen concentrate, albumin and Anti-D are human plasma derived. Individual patient acceptance still requires discussion.

questions.stem: An adult patient undergoing cardiac surgery exhibits excessive bleeding following cardiopulmonary bypass. A thromboelastogram performed on their blood is shown below. The most likely cause of the bleeding is

opts.why: EXTEM includes platelet and fibrin contributions. A preserved FIBTEM with reduced EXTEM clot strength implicates the platelet component; confirm with local thresholds and clinical bleeding.
A preserved FIBTEM amplitude argues against isolated fibrinogen depletion.
Hyperfibrinolysis requires a lysis pattern, not just low early EXTEM amplitude.
Residual heparin primarily prolongs clotting time; heparinase comparison is needed.
An EXTEM A5 of 22 mm is reduced, not normal.

questions.expl: EXTEM incorporates platelet plus fibrin contributions; low EXTEM amplitude with preserved FIBTEM favours impaired platelet contribution; fibrinogen depletion lowers FIBTEM, fibrinolysis needs lysis indices, and residual heparin changes clotting time.

questions.stem: A term neonate is undergoing closure of gastroschisis under general anaesthesia with pressure control ventilation via an endotracheal tube. The estimated blood loss is 10 mL. Fluid therapy has been 4% albumin 40 mL/kg in addition to maintenance 10% dextrose 4 mL/kg/h. During closure of the defect, the oxygen saturation falls to 80%. The most likely cause of the desaturation is

opts.why: Incorrect in this scenario: pulmonary fluid overload is possible in neonates, but it does not specifically explain the immediate deterioration coinciding with abdominal reduction.
Reduction of viscera raises intra-abdominal pressure and splints the diaphragm, lowering compliance; with pressure-control ventilation, delivered tidal volume can decline.
An unrecognised congenital cardiac lesion does not explain a new event tightly coupled to abdominal closure.
Not the best explanation: pulmonary hypertension can cause hypoxaemia but abdominal restriction is the directly supported mechanism during this manoeuvre.

questions.expl: The Society for Pediatric Anesthesia case guide specifically notes higher inspiratory pressure is needed after abdominal reduction due to decreased thoracic compliance. In pressure-control mode tidal volume may fall.

questions.stem: Phaeochromocytoma commonly presents with all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Correct (least characteristic): isolated RV hypertrophy more commonly signals chronic RV pressure/volume loading; it is not a typical direct manifestation of catecholamine excess in uncomplicated phaeochromocytoma.
Sinus tachycardia is a recognised consequence of excess catecholamines.
QT prolongation is a documented repolarisation abnormality.
ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities can accompany catecholamine effects or myocardial injury.
Catecholamine-associated cardiomyopathy, including stress-type dysfunction, is recognised.

questions.expl: A review of phaeochromocytoma cardiac manifestations describes sinus tachycardia, QT and ST-T changes, and catecholamine-associated cardiomyopathy; isolated RV hypertrophy is not a characteristic direct effect. This tests the revised practice wording, not historical options.

questions.stem: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is NOT associated with

opts.why: Very high serum creatine kinase is characteristic of dystrophin-related muscle injury.
Some female carriers have cardiomyopathy; surveillance is recommended in Duchenne care guidelines.

opts.t: Reduced sensitivity to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers
opts.why: Correct (NOT associated): reduced sensitivity is the opposite of the commonly reported increased sensitivity and prolonged neuromuscular blockade in DMD.
DMD is caused by pathogenic variants affecting dystrophin.
Suxamethonium and certain anaesthetic exposures carry anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalaemia risk in dystrophinopathies.

questions.expl: 2025 ESAIC/ESPA guidelines specifically report increased sensitivity/prolonged recovery with nondepolarising blockade; DMD care guidance confirms female-carrier cardiomyopathy and other systemic features.

questions.stem: When administered in combination with tramadol, the agent considered highest risk for the development of serotonin syndrome is

opts.why: Moclobemide is a reversible MAO-A inhibitor; its combination with tramadol is contraindicated because of high serotonin-toxicity risk.
Incorrect as the highest-risk choice: escitalopram (SSRI) increases risk with tramadol but the MAOI combination is the stronger contraindication.
Incorrect as highest-risk: desvenlafaxine (SNRI) is a relevant serotonergic co-medication, but the MAOI is the uniquely high-risk choice here.
Tapentadol is not an MAOI. It is not equivalent to an MAOI–tramadol interaction, although serotonergic adverse events still merit caution.

questions.expl: Medsafe classifies tramadol–MAOI as a contraindicated high-risk combination. Moclobemide SmPC explicitly contraindicates co-administration with tramadol; SSRIs/SNRIs also carry risk but lower class-tier here.

questions.stem: The action of methylene blue in treating vasoplegia is mediated by

opts.t: Inhibition of nitric oxide synthase and soluble guanylate cyclase, reducing cGMP signalling
opts.why: Methylene blue reduces NO–cGMP-mediated vasodilatation through sGC and NOS-related effects; it is not a direct alpha/vasopressin/angiotensin agonist.
Methylene blue does not act as a direct α1-adrenoceptor agonist.
Its effect is not selective V1-receptor agonism.
It is not a direct AT1-receptor agonist.
Β1 stimulation would primarily affect cardiac activity and is not its vasoplegia mechanism.

questions.expl: Methylene blue reduces NO–cGMP-mediated vasodilatation through sGC and NOS-related effects; it is not a direct alpha/vasopressin/angiotensin agonist. Evidence check: NO-sGC pathway vs receptor agonists; original mechanistic item may have >1 true mechanism

questions.stem: A stellate ganglion block is NOT indicated in the management of

opts.why: Ordinary atrioventricular conduction block is not treated by stellate sympathetic block; pacing and cause-directed management are relevant.
Left stellate block is used in selected refractory ventricular arrhythmias/electrical storm.
PTSD has been investigated as an off-label indication, though not established routine practice.
Vasospastic symptoms such as Raynaud phenomenon, which may occur in scleroderma, are among sympathetic-block applications.
Sympathetically driven hyperhidrosis is a documented use.

questions.expl: Clinical review lists ventricular arrhythmias, Raynaud/vasospastic disorders, hyperhidrosis and investigational PTSD as SGB uses; ordinary AV conduction block is not. PTSD and scleroderma uses are not established routine indications, so practice stem specifies documented or investigational.

questions.stem: Obstructive sleep apnoea in children is diagnosed with an apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) of at least

opts.why: The BTS 2023 guideline classifies mild paediatric OSA at OAHI ≥1 and <5 events/hour.
Incorrect as the lower threshold: OAHI ≥5 indicates at least moderate paediatric OSA.
Incorrect as the lower threshold: OAHI ≥10 is in the severe category.
OAHI 15 is far above the diagnostic threshold and is also severe.

questions.expl: 2023 British Thoracic Society criterion for children <16: mild paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea begins at OAHI ≥1/hr. OAHI is obstructive events, unlike undifferentiated AHI.

questions.stem: Neostigmine should be avoided in patients with

opts.why: Familial periodic paralysis involves altered muscle excitability, not the classic neostigmine-provoked myotonic contracture.
Myotonia congenita is a chloride-channel myotonic disease; neostigmine may worsen myotonic contractions.
Not best: DMD has increased sensitivity to nondepolarising relaxants and prolonged recovery, but myotonia congenita is the specific condition associated with anticholinesterase-induced myotonia.
Not best: Becker dystrophy is a dystrophinopathy and not a classical myotonic channelopathy.
Friedreich ataxia is not defined by anticholinesterase-provoked myotonic contracture.

questions.expl: 2025 ESAIC/ESPA recommends caution/avoidance of neostigmine in myotonic disorders because it may worsen myotonia; other listed diseases may also need careful reversal but do not have that same characteristic precipitated contracture.

questions.stem: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure is contraindicated in patients with

opts.why: TIPS is used selectively in hepatorenal syndrome/portal hypertensive complications.
Refractory ascites is an established indication for selected candidates.
Severe untreated valvular heart disease / right-sided cardiac dysfunction contraindicates elective TIPS. The other options are potential TIPS indications.
Recurrent or refractory variceal bleeding is an important indication.
Budd–Chiari syndrome can be managed with TIPS in selected cases.

questions.expl: Severe untreated valvular heart disease / right-sided cardiac dysfunction contraindicates elective TIPS. The other options are potential TIPS indications. Evidence check: Severe TR is an absolute contraindication; others are indications in selected patients

questions.stem: When confirming correct placement of an endotracheal tube, verifying the presence of sustained exhaled carbon dioxide requires all the

opts.t: CO2 rises on expiration and falls on inspiration
opts.why: Incorrect as EXCEPT: expiratory CO₂ rise and inspiratory fall is required.
Correct (EXCEPT): a consistently square capnogram is not required; waveform morphology may differ with obstruction or other clinical circumstances.
Incorrect as EXCEPT: nondeclining amplitude across at least seven breaths is an explicit criterion.
Incorrect as EXCEPT: a peak more than 1 kPa (7.5 mmHg) above baseline is required.
Incorrect as EXCEPT: the waveform/value must fit the clinical context.

questions.expl: RCoA page quotes all four PUMA criteria for sustained exhaled CO2: expiratory rise/inspiratory fall, nondeclining ≥7 breaths, peak >1kPa above baseline, and appropriate clinical reading; square plateau not mandated.

questions.stem: The dataset that was used to create the Eleveld TCI model did NOT include patients who are / have

opts.why: The Eleveld development material included neonates/very young infants.
Older adults were included in the pooled dataset.
Patients with liver cirrhosis were included in a contributing dataset.
Development cohort included people down to 27 weeks postmenstrual age, older adults and cirrhotic patients. Neonates are NOT the correct exclusion; no ESRD cohort identified in development.

questions.expl: Development cohort included people down to 27 weeks postmenstrual age, older adults and cirrhotic patients. Neonates are NOT the correct exclusion; no ESRD cohort identified in development.

questions.stem: The blood product that contains the highest concentration of citrate is

opts.why: FFP delivers anticoagulant citrate in its plasma volume; washed RBC and purified concentrates deliver much less. Exact citrate concentration cannot be ranked without component specifications.
Washed RBCs have much of the storage supernatant and anticoagulant removed, unlike plasma.
Recombinant FVIIa is not transfused as citrated plasma.
Normal saline contains no citrate.
Purified fibrinogen concentrate is not a major routine citrated plasma-volume load.

questions.expl: Fresh frozen plasma carries citrate-containing anticoagulated plasma; washed RBC have reduced plasma supernatant, while recombinant/purified products and saline do not supply equivalent plasma citrate.

questions.stem: During a new pandemic, an anaesthetist refuses to provide sedation for an elective operation due to concern that the procedure may hasten community spread of the disease. This is the ethical principle of

opts.why: Beneficence concerns acting to promote benefit; the stem centres on preventing harm.

Non-maleficence is the obligation to avoid foreseeable harm. Distributive justice could also become relevant in resource-allocation examples; this practice version deliberately identifies avoidable harm as its focus.
Distributive justice concerns fair allocation of resources/benefits.
Autonomy concerns respecting informed patient choices, not this third-party harm issue.
Veracity means honesty/truthfulness.

questions.expl: Non-maleficence specifically means avoiding harm; beneficence promotes benefit, distributive justice concerns fair allocation, autonomy respects independent choice, and veracity concerns truth-telling.

questions.stem: The anaesthetic technique associated with the highest rate of postprocedure patency of a newly-created arteriovenous fistula is

opts.why: Propofol TIVA has no comparable local sympathectomy causing fistula-vein vasodilation.
Randomised data show improved fistula primary patency with regional block compared with local anaesthesia at 12 months (79% vs 59%).
Infiltration plus sedation lacks the brachial-plexus sympathetic blockade effect.
A volatile GA does not reliably reproduce regional sympathectomy-related flow improvement.

questions.expl: The comparative trial of brachial plexus regional anaesthesia for AV fistula creation demonstrates improved patency versus local anaesthesia; alternatives lack the same vasodilatory regional effect.

questions.stem: The image below shows the arterial pressure (red, upper line) and balloon pressure (blue, lower line) from an intra-aortic balloon pump set at 1:2 augmentation. The point of the waveform indicated by the large green arrow is called

opts.why: Rapid pre-systolic deflation reduces aortic end-diastolic pressure; the trough preceding the next assisted systole is assisted end-diastolic pressure.
Unassisted systolic pressure is the peak of an unassisted beat, not the pressure immediately after balloon deflation.
Diastolic augmentation is the peak after inflation, not the trough following deflation.
Unassisted end-diastolic pressure refers to a beat without balloon assistance.
Assisted systolic pressure is the ensuing systolic peak rather than the pre-systolic end-diastolic value.

questions.expl: Rapid IABP balloon deflation lowers aortic end-diastolic pressure before assisted systole; diastolic augmentation precedes deflation and unassisted systole is a different beat.

questions.stem: A patient’s true arterial oxygen saturation will be lower than a pulse oximeter reading in the presence of

opts.why: Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO2 can appear falsely reassuring relative to true arterial oxyhaemoglobin saturation. Confirm by blood co-oximetry.
Sickle-cell trait by itself does not systematically cause this characteristic SpO₂ overestimate.
Methylene blue more typically produces an erroneously LOW pulse-oximeter reading.

opts.t: Severe anaemia with normal oxyhaemoglobin saturation
opts.why: Severe anaemia lowers oxygen content but need not lower fractional saturation when gas exchange is normal.

questions.expl: Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, falsely increasing SpO2 relative to true oxyhaemoglobin saturation. Methylene blue generally causes falsely reduced readings.

questions.stem: Organ procurement after circulatory deathdraft is generally stood down if the time from cessation of cardiorespiratory support to circulatory death extends beyond

opts.why: The given programme explicitly allows an agonal interval longer than 30 minutes.
60 minutes is shorter than its stated 90-minute maximum.
A 90-minute stand-down applies in some ANZ DCD pathways, but donor/organ-specific warm-ischaemia constraints and local policy supersede any universal timing assertion.
By 120 minutes the stated 90-minute stand-down limit has already passed.
180 minutes likewise exceeds the specified policy window.

questions.expl: A 90-minute stand-down applies in some ANZ DCD pathways, but donor/organ-specific warm-ischaemia constraints and local policy supersede any universal timing assertion. Evidence check: ANZICS 2021, §2.4.3: ~90-min customary agonal stand-down; organ-specific exceptions

questions.stem: The rank of volatile anaesthetic agents from highest to lowest derived global warming potential over 100 years (GWP100) is

opts.why: This incorrectly puts nitrous oxide above desflurane for 100-year GWP per kilogram of agent.
On a mass basis the approximate GWP100 ordering is desflurane > isoflurane > nitrous oxide > sevoflurane; this is not an equal-MAC comparison.
Nitrous oxide has a lower per-mass GWP100 than isoflurane, so this middle order is wrong.
Desflurane, not nitrous oxide, is highest among the listed agents; isoflurane also exceeds sevoflurane.

questions.expl: For 100-year greenhouse warming potential per unit mass the order is desflurane > isoflurane > nitrous oxide > sevoflurane; this is not the same as climate impact at clinically equivalent doses.

questions.stem: A characteristic feature of postoperative visual loss due to posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is

opts.why: Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy classically causes painless visual loss.
An afferent pupillary defect may occur with optic-nerve ischaemia; intact light reflex is not the characteristic discriminator.
Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy produces painless vision loss with initially normal optic disc/fundus; an afferent pupil defect may be present.
Visual inattention suggests cortical/attentional pathology rather than optic neuropathy.

questions.expl: Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy produces painless vision loss with initially normal optic disc/fundus; an afferent pupil defect may be present. Evidence check: PION is painless with initially normal fundus and possible RAPD

questions.stem: The bipolar leads of a 12-lead electrocardiogram are

opts.why: The 12 leads include precordial and augmented leads, not all conventionally called bipolar limb leads.
V1–V6 are precordial leads referenced to the central terminal.
Augmented aVR/aVL/aVF are not the standard Einthoven bipolar limb leads.

opts.t: Limb leads I, II and III
opts.why: I, II, III directly compare two limb electrode potentials in the conventional nomenclature.
Einthoven leads I, II, III are conventionally bipolar.

questions.expl: The AHA statement identifies standard limb leads I, II and III as conventional Einthoven leads. Technical caveat: augmented and precordial leads are also effectively differential electrically, so wording specifies the historical classification.

questions.stem: The local anaesthetic with the lowest CC/CNS ratio (ratio of the drug dose required to cause cardiac collapse to the drug dose required to cause seizure) is

opts.why: Levobupivacaine has a comparatively larger cardiac-collapse/CNS-toxicity separation than racemic bupivacaine.
Racemic bupivacaine has the narrowest separation between seizure and cardiovascular collapse of the listed agents.
Lignocaine has a wider cardiotoxicity margin.
Ropivacaine is generally less cardiotoxic than racemic bupivacaine at clinically comparable exposures.

questions.expl: Racemic bupivacaine has the narrowest separation between seizure and cardiovascular collapse of the listed agents. Evidence check: CC:CNS ratio lowest for racemic bupivacaine among choices

questions.stem: The time for reversal of therapeutic dabigatran after administration of idarucizumab 5 g is

opts.why: Idarucizumab binds circulating dabigatran and removes its anticoagulant effect within minutes; 5 min is the earliest listed approximation, not a mandatory delay.
15 min is later than the nearly immediate reversal reported after idarucizumab dosing.
30 min is later than the expected pharmacodynamic reversal; ongoing clinical bleeding may persist for other reasons.
60 min is not the usual onset interval for drug neutralisation.
120 min overstates the expected time for drug neutralisation, although repeat levels may be needed if dabigatran redistributes.

questions.expl: Idarucizumab binds dabigatran rapidly; lab reversal is evident immediately after administration. '5 minutes' is the shortest listed approximation, not an exact required wait. Evidence check: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran immediately; 5 minutes is earliest listed option, not fixed universal pharmacodynamic delay

questions.stem: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx do NOT include

opts.why: Incorrect as exception: cricothyroid is intrinsic despite its distinctive superior-laryngeal-nerve motor supply.
Correct exception: suprahyoid muscles attach outside the larynx and are extrinsic elevators.
The transverse arytenoid is an intrinsic (unpaired) laryngeal muscle.
Posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles are intrinsic.

questions.expl: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles include cricothyroid, transverse arytenoid and both cricoarytenoids; suprahyoid muscles are extrinsic elevators.

questions.stem: When interpreting an arterial blood gas, a high serum anion gap is consistent with

opts.why: Not typical: lithium toxicity is not a classic primary cause of high anion-gap metabolic acidosis in the absence of another process.
Salicylate overdose can produce high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis together with respiratory alkalosis.
Hyperchloraemic acidosis usually has a normal anion gap.
Hypoalbuminaemia reduces the measured anion gap and can mask a raised gap.
Hypercalcaemia is not itself a typical cause of raised anion gap.

questions.expl: Salicylate toxicity classically produces a mixed respiratory alkalosis and high anion-gap metabolic acidosis; hyperchloraemia is associated with normal-gap acidosis; hypoalbuminaemia lowers the measured gap.

questions.stem: The Glasgow Blatchford score is used to risk stratify

opts.why: Pulmonary haemorrhage is not the target condition for this score.
Intraperitoneal trauma has other haemorrhage assessment tools.
Postpartum haemorrhage uses obstetric-specific clinical scoring/assessment.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage has neurological grading systems, not Glasgow-Blatchford.
Glasgow-Blatchford stratifies upper gastrointestinal bleeding before endoscopy.

questions.expl: ACG guideline endorses Glasgow-Blatchford score in upper GI bleeding to identify very-low-risk patients for outpatient follow-up.

questions.stem: In a male patient with quadriplegia undergoing a rigid cystoscopy, the optimal choice of anaesthesia to prevent autonomic dysreflexia is

opts.why: Adequate neuraxial blockade interrupts afferent input and may prevent autonomic dysreflexia during cystoscopy. A functioning spinal block can prevent autonomic dysreflexia during lower urinary tract procedures; assess if procedure or patient factors change the preferred approach.
Epidural blockade can work but may be less reliably dense/rapid than spinal blockade for a short potent stimulus.
A single fixed MAC does not guarantee abolition of noxious afferent input or dysreflexia.
Topical anaesthesia alone often fails to block bladder distension-related afferents.

questions.expl: Effective spinal anaesthesia can block the autonomic dysreflexia reflex arc during cystoscopy in high SCI; epidural can be patchy, one-MAC GA does not guarantee protection, and topical alone is unreliable.

questions.stem: Interference with pacemaker function can result from all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: RF ablation can interfere with pacemaker sensing/function.
Monopolar diathermy close to a generator can generate EMI.
Defibrillation can affect implanted devices and merits precautions/interrogation.
Routine CT generally carries lower interference risk than RF/electrosurgical energy. It is not completely risk-free: rare transient CT-related device effects are recognised.
Surgical high-frequency cautery is a recognised EMI risk.

questions.expl: Routine diagnostic CT rarely creates clinically significant CIED interference; electrocautery, MRI and radiotherapy pose more relevant device-specific risks. Avoid claiming CT has absolutely zero risk.

questions.stem: A neonate with a postmenstrual age of 34 weeks (born at 26 weeks) and weighing 2 kg is undergoing retinal laser therapy under general anaesthesia. The oxygen saturation is 92% on the following ventilator settings: FiO2 0.4; inspiratory pressure 15 cmH2O; PEEP 5 cmH2O; rate 24 breaths per minute. The most appropriate course of action is to

opts.why: Increasing FiO₂ to 1.0 exposes a preterm neonate to unnecessary hyperoxia risk when within the target range.
Routine suction without evidence of obstruction risks disturbance and is not triggered by SpO₂ 92%.
Higher PEEP is not justified without mechanics/oxygenation evidence of recruitment need.
A high-pressure recruitment manoeuvre risks barotrauma without an indication.
Interpret by postmenstrual age, retinopathy phase and local saturation targets. SpO2 of 92% is within usual preterm neonatal oxygen saturation targets, but FiO2 and gestational context matter.

questions.expl: At 34 weeks postmenstrual age, SpO2 92% generally lies in neonatal target range around 91–95%; without clinical deterioration, escalation to FiO2 1.0, suction or recruitment is unwarranted.

questions.stem: When auscultating the heart the Valsalva manoeuvre will increase the murmur intensity of

opts.why: Aortic stenosis typically becomes softer with reduced preload during Valsalva strain.
Mitral stenosis generally does not intensify as a classic Valsalva response.
Mitral regurgitation typically decreases with strain-reduced venous return.
Decreased preload during Valsalva accentuates the click/murmur of MVP; HOCM also intensifies but is not offered.
VSD flow murmur usually decreases with lower venous return/preload.

questions.expl: Valsalva reduces preload, causing earlier prolapse and a longer/louder mitral-valve prolapse murmur; AS and most MR decrease with preload reduction.

questions.stem: The most appropriate order of blood products transfused sequentially through the same blood administration set is

opts.why: RBC first risks exposing subsequent platelets to debris from an RBC-used set.
Again platelets follow RBCs through the used set, which is not advised.
Platelets follow RBCs and thus encounter a previously RBC-used administration set.

Platelets should be administered via a new set and must not follow RBCs through an RBC-used set. D is the only candidate that avoids this in the recovered options; ordering of plasma separately is not itself prescribed.

questions.expl: Platelets should be administered via a new set and must not follow RBCs through an RBC-used set. D is the only candidate that avoids this in the recovered options; ordering of plasma separately is not itself prescribed.

questions.stem: The breathing system shown in the accompanying picture is an example of Mapleson

opts.why: Mapleson A includes longer tubing and a characteristic distal fresh-gas inlet.
Mapleson B shares arrangement but has elongated corrugated tubing.
Mapleson C is compact, omitting elongated corrugated tubing.
Mapleson D has fresh gas delivered at the patient end and APL near the bag/machine.
Mapleson F is a Jackson-Rees modification without the same APL arrangement.

questions.expl: Mapleson C is a shortened Mapleson B with the reservoir bag/APL near the patient and no elongated corrugated tube; alternative circuits differ in inlet/valve placement.

questions.stem: In an anaesthetised patient with anaphylaxis, cardiac compression should be initiated at a systolic blood pressure of less than

opts.why: <40 mmHg is below the specified <50 mmHg action threshold, delaying compressions.
ANZAAG–ANZCA specifies start compressions when systolic pressure is below 50 mmHg, even if monitoring still detects cardiac activity.
<60 mmHg is a less severe threshold than the card stipulates.
<80 mmHg is not the specific ANZAAG trigger.
<100 mmHg is not the specific trigger.

questions.expl: ANZAAG–ANZCA specifies start compressions when systolic pressure is below 50 mmHg, even if monitoring still detects cardiac activity.

questions.stem: The muscle recommended for neuromuscular monitoring by the 2023 American Society of Anesthesiologists practice guidelines is the

opts.why: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring at adductor pollicis is the recommended reference for assessment of recovery and extubation.
Flexor pollicis longus is not the standard site used for quantitative adductor-pollicis recovery assessment.
A foot muscle is not the guideline-preferred recovery monitoring site.
Corrugator supercilii can track onset but is not preferred for confirming recovery.
Orbicularis oculi may overestimate recovery compared with adductor pollicis.

questions.expl: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring at adductor pollicis is the recommended reference for assessment of recovery and extubation. Evidence check: 2023 ASA guideline strong recommendation for adductor pollicis and against eye muscles

questions.stem: A single intraoperative dose of 8 mg dexamethasone compared to 4 mg results in

opts.t: 8 mg has substantially higher PONV efficacy in every population
opts.why: Direct comparisons have not established an across-the-board major PONV advantage of 8 mg.

opts.t: No clinically important additional PONV prevention from 8 mg compared with 4 mg
opts.why: Direct-comparison meta-analysis finds little additional PONV efficacy from larger doses; analgesia, hyperglycaemia and other outcomes are separate questions.
Dexamethasone can increase glucose transiently; 8 mg does not prevent that.
Increased infection is not a reliably demonstrated consequence of one antiemetic dose.
Four milligrams has proven antiemetic activity.

questions.expl: Direct-dose comparisons show little additional PONV prevention from 8 vs 4 mg dexamethasone; neither dose abolishes PONV, prevents hyperglycaemia, or uniformly raises infection risk.

questions.stem: You are undertaking an ultrasound guided pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block for hip surgery. In the accompanying image, the structure labelled with the arrow is the

opts.why: The PENG target is deep to the iliopsoas tendon adjacent to the iliopubic eminence.
Sartorius arises from ASIS, not the PENG injection plane.
Rectus femoris is anterior hip musculature but not the described target.
Pectineus is medial/anterior thigh and not immediately over the iliopubic eminence injection point.
TFL is lateral to the relevant iliopsoas target.

questions.expl: PENG local anaesthetic is deposited under the iliopsoas/psoas tendon on the superior pubic ramus at iliopubic eminence; none of the other listed tendons marks this target.

questions.stem: The tooth most commonly damaged during direct laryngoscopy is the

opts.why: Incorrect as most frequent: right central maxillary incisor is at risk, but the left is most commonly reported with laryngoscope pressure.
Lateral incisors are less frequently implicated than maxillary central incisors.
The left maxillary central incisor is frequently contacted by the laryngoscope blade.
The right maxillary lateral incisor is not the commonest reported tooth.

questions.expl: Review of peri-anaesthetic dental injuries identifies the left maxillary central incisor as the most frequently damaged individual tooth during laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: In the event of an electrical fire in the operating room, the correct fire extinguisher type to use is

opts.why: Powder may be less suitable around electrical equipment and creates contamination.
Water conducts electricity and is inappropriate for energised electrical fires.
Foam/water-based agents are unsuitable for energised electrical equipment.

Stop gases and ignition first; extinguisher type depends on local electrical/fire protocol. CO2 is appropriate for energized electrical equipment; theatre fire management prioritises stopping gases/power where feasible and patient rescue.

questions.expl: CO2 extinguishers avoid conducting electricity and are suitable for energized electrical equipment. Water/foam are less suitable for live energized devices; powder may damage equipment.

questions.stem: According to the ISO colour code for medical gas cylinders, Entonox is indicated by

opts.why: Contemporary Australia/NZ gas mix cylinder shoulder coding confirmed. Historical ISO colour coding for nitrous oxide–oxygen mix is blue/white. Verify jurisdiction, cylinder body/shoulder and current labelling.
Yellow is not the conventional Entonox cylinder colour combination.
Black alone is not Entonox's blue/white identification.
Grey is not Entonox's specified colour code.

questions.expl: In Australia/NZ the 50:50 nitrous oxide/oxygen Entonox cylinder is identifiable by blue and white marking, unlike single-gas cylinders.

questions.stem: During resuscitation of a newborn, the heart rate is noted to be 50 beats per minute despite optimal ventilation and chest compressions. The next step in management is to give intravenous adrenaline

opts.why: 1:1000 is 1 mg/mL, a 10-fold higher concentration than intended for this IV volume.
0.5–1 mL/kg of 1:10,000 exceeds the recommended initial dose.
ANZCOR 13.7 recommends IV adrenaline 10–30 micrograms/kg (0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000) if HR remains <60 despite adequate ventilation and compressions.
1:100,000 is tenfold more dilute than the guideline concentration.

questions.expl: ANZCOR 13.7 recommends IV adrenaline 10–30 micrograms/kg (0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000) if HR remains <60 despite adequate ventilation and compressions.

questions.stem: An adult weighing 80 kg has sustained full-thickness burns to 40% of their body. The recommended volume of fluid resuscitation in the first 24

opts.why: 6,400 mL reflects 2 mL/kg/%TBSA, below the specified 3 mL formula.
Australian/New Zealand modified Parkland initial estimate, titrated to response; ABA uses 2 mL/kg/%TBSA.
12,800 mL uses 4 mL/kg/%TBSA rather than 3.
16,000 mL uses 5 mL/kg/%TBSA.
19,200 mL uses 6 mL/kg/%TBSA.

questions.expl: Australian/New Zealand modified Parkland initial estimate, titrated to response; ABA uses 2 mL/kg/%TBSA.

questions.stem: In a can’t intubate, can’t oxygenate (CICO) scenario when using a 14G cannula and a Rapid-O2 oxygen delivery device, the initial rescue breath should be

opts.why: Both 10 L/min flow and 2 seconds differ from this device's cited initial setting.
Four seconds at 10 L/min uses a lower flow than specified.
Fifteen L/min is right but 2 seconds is not the specified initial insufflation.
The Rapid-O₂ instructions specify approximately 4 seconds initial insufflation at 15 L/min; subsequent insufflation/expiration are reassessed by chest movement, not delivered blindly.
Ten seconds risks excessive delivered gas/pressure and is not the initial recommendation.

questions.expl: The Rapid-O₂ instructions specify approximately 4 seconds initial insufflation at 15 L/min; subsequent insufflation/expiration are reassessed by chest movement, not delivered blindly. Propylthiouracil is a thionamide used for hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion control.

questions.stem: A patient with a perioperative troponin rise above normal, chest pain, left ventricular anterior regional wall motion abnormality, and atheroma without thrombus occluding 70% of the left anterior descending coronary artery has had a/an

opts.t: Acute myocardial infarction, with type 1 versus type 2 not yet established

Dynamic troponin with ischaemic features is not chronic stable myocardial injury.

Troponin rise/fall exceeding the 99th percentile demonstrates acute myocardial injury.

questions.stem: A patient who underwent a thoracotomy six months ago reports shooting pain on the chest wall occurring without any trigger. This is known as

Hypoaesthesia means reduced sensation.

questions.stem: A drug which is unlikely to interfere with skin testing is oral

opts.why: Diphenhydramine is an H1 antihistamine and suppresses immediate wheal responses.
Amitriptyline has important H1-antagonist properties and can reduce skin-test reactivity.
Short-course systemic oral prednisolone generally does not materially suppress immediate IgE skin-prick wheals; prolonged/high-dose exposure can be more nuanced.
Cetirizine is an H1 antihistamine that suppresses immediate skin-prick wheals (newly authored distractor; NOT from historical recall).
Ranitidine is an H2 antagonist and can cause a smaller reduction in wheal size; effects are less substantial than typical H1 blockers.

questions.expl: A short course of systemic prednisolone generally does not materially suppress immediate skin-prick wheals. H1 antagonists (diphenhydramine, cetirizine, amitriptyline) do; H2 blockers can modestly suppress responses. Evidence check: Short-course usual oral steroid generally does not suppress immediate prick responses; antihistaminergic drugs do. AAAAI link may require checking variant spelling.

questions.stem: According to the ANZCA guideline on fatigue risk management in anaesthesia practice the duration of an ideal nap is

opts.why: ANZCA's main PG43(A) recommendation for a nap DURING a night shift is 20–30 min; a separate background infographic says 10–20 min 'ideal' in a different context.
ANZCA PG43(A) 2020 recommends a 20–30-minute during-shift nap.
30–40 minutes extends beyond the stated short-nap window and can increase sleep inertia.
40–50 minutes is not the recommended short restorative nap and may increase sleep inertia.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old requires anaesthesia for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. They have a history of mastocytosis and have never had an anaesthetic in the past. The non- depolarising muscle relaxant to avoid using is

opts.why: Patient-specific allergy management is important; no NMBA can be automatically called risk-free. Atracurium can release histamine; with mastocytosis use individual risk assessment and allergy history.
Cisatracurium has relatively little direct histamine release compared with atracurium.
Pancuronium is not classically a high histamine releaser.
Rocuronium can cause IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, but atracurium is singled out here for non-IgE histamine release.
Vecuronium is relatively low histamine-releasing; individual drug allergy remains possible.

questions.expl: Histamine releasing drugs such as atracurium warrant caution in mastocytosis; the other listed drugs do not share the same well-known direct mast-cell-degranulation profile.

questions.stem: A healthy woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy has an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status classification of

opts.why: Pregnancy itself gives a healthy uncomplicated parturient ASA II rather than ASA I under ASA examples.
Normal pregnancy is ASA II by current ASA classification examples.
ASA III requires a severe systemic disease or substantial functional limitation.
ASA IV indicates severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life.

questions.expl: Normal pregnancy is ASA II by current ASA classification examples.

questions.stem: The antibiotic considered safest to be administered to a patient with myasthenia gravis in the perioperative period is

opts.why: Not the best: vancomycin has reported neuromuscular effects and is not the uncomplicated first choice here.
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside and can impair neuromuscular transmission.
Erythromycin is a macrolide associated with MG exacerbation.
Flucloxacillin, a penicillin-class beta-lactam, is not among the classic antibiotic classes aggravating MG.
Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone with recognized MG exacerbation warnings.

questions.expl: Medsafe lists aminoglycosides, macrolides and fluoroquinolones as potential MG exacerbants. A beta-lactam such as flucloxacillin is preferable among this set; vancomycin can also have neuromuscular interaction concerns.

questions.stem: The clinical laser type with the greatest tissue penetration is

opts.why: Argon laser light is absorbed more superficially than 1064-nm Nd:YAG in typical soft tissues.
Nd:YAG 1064nm has the greatest tissue penetration of the listed lasers.
Er:YAG is strongly water absorbed and very superficial.
CO₂ is strongly water absorbed, producing shallow surface penetration.
Holmium:YAG at ~2100nm penetrates substantially less deeply than Nd:YAG.

questions.expl: Comparison of optical penetration into human skin: Nd:YAG 1064nm ~3.39mm exceeds argon ~0.8–0.95mm, Ho:YAG ~0.4mm, Er:YAG and CO2 only micrometres.

questions.stem: The accompanying image is obtained while doing an ultrasound guided erector spinae plane block at the level of the transverse process of the fourth thoracic vertebra. The muscle marked by the arrow is the

opts.why: Trapezius lies more superficial than the erector spinae layer.
Rhomboid major may be visible at T4, but lies superficial to erector spinae.
Erector spinae muscle is immediately superficial to the transverse-process target plane.
Latissimus dorsi is not the deep muscle contacting the transverse process at the injection plane.
Serratus anterior lies laterally on the thoracic wall, not the posterior transverse-process plane.

questions.stem: Risk factors for delirium after hip fracture surgery include all EXCEPT

opts.why: Frailty is a clinical risk factor, not a randomised anaesthesia assignment in the REGAIN trial.
Older age is a risk factor but was not the randomised exposure in REGAIN.
The trial randomised spinal versus general anaesthesia and found similar delirium incidence (20.5% versus 19.7%). Observational cohort associations do not prove a causal difference.
Sex was not the randomised assignment; male sex has been associated with delirium in observational hip-fracture cohorts.

questions.expl: REGAIN randomised anaesthetic technique and found delirium 20.5% after spinal versus 19.7% after general anaesthesia (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.84–1.30). Age, sex and frailty were not randomised comparators. Observational studies may still associate GA with delirium. Evidence check: REGAIN RCT found no overall delirium difference with spinal vs GA, BUT a 2026 observational meta-analysis associated GA with delirium; original risk-factor stem remains uncertain.

questions.stem: The effects of empagliflozin include a decrease in

opts.why: SGLT2 inhibitors can promote ketogenesis and euglycaemic DKA risk, not reliably decrease it.
SGLT2 inhibitor glycosuria causes osmotic diuresis and volume depletion. SGLT2 inhibition increases glycosuria and osmotic diuresis; serum creatinine may transiently rise.
Creatinine may transiently rise and should not be assumed to fall.
Blocking renal SGLT2 raises urinary glucose excretion; it does not reduce glycosuria.

questions.expl: SGLT2 inhibition causes glycosuria, osmotic diuresis and associated reduction in circulating fluid volume, not increased insulin secretion or volume expansion.

questions.stem: Oral naltrexone should be ceased preoperatively for

opts.why: 24 h is generally too short for oral naltrexone receptor blockade to wane before anticipated opioid analgesia.
48 h may still leave clinically relevant antagonism; 72 h is commonly recommended.

Perioperative systemic opioid analgesia may be blocked if naltrexone recently administered. Usual planned opioid anaesthesia interruption interval for oral naltrexone is ~72h; consider individual dose and relapse risks.
96 h is longer than the standard cited 72-hour interval for oral formulation (individualisation possible).

questions.expl: Perioperative systemic opioid analgesia may be blocked if naltrexone recently administered. Usual planned opioid anaesthesia interruption interval for oral naltrexone is ~72h; consider individual dose and relapse risks.

questions.stem: A medication that has NOT been associated with arrhythmogenic potential in patients with Brugada syndrome is

opts.why: Prolonged/high-dose propofol infusion has historically raised concern in Brugada; short routine use has different evidence.
Thiopentone is the historically cited choice. Short carefully monitored propofol induction is also supported by newer studies, so it must not be portrayed as always contraindicated.
Large ketamine infusions are not the traditional preferred comparator in Brugada.
Isoprenaline is an arrhythmia treatment rather than an induction agent.
Flecainide is a sodium-channel blocker and may unmask/worsen Brugada; it is not a routine induction drug.

questions.expl: Thiopentone is a historically accepted induction option for Brugada, while prolonged/high-dose propofol was traditionally cautioned; modern evidence does not support automatically banning single-dose propofol.

questions.stem: Borders of the anterior triangle of the neck DO NOT include the

opts.why: Incorrect as EXCEPT: the inferior mandibular border is the anterior triangle's superior boundary.
Correct exception: middle third of clavicle forms part of the posterior triangle boundary, not the anterior triangle.
Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid bounds the anterior triangle laterally.
The neck's midline is the medial border of the anterior triangle.

questions.expl: The anterior triangle boundaries are inferior mandibular border, anterior sternocleidomastoid margin and neck midline; clavicle marks the inferior boundary of the posterior triangle.

questions.stem: In a patient presenting with an Addisonian crisis, the electrolyte disturbances MOST LIKELY to be seen are

opts.why: Incorrect as most typical: hypocalcaemia is not a defining adrenal-crisis biochemical feature.
Hyperglycaemia is not the typical cortisol-deficiency glucose derangement.
Hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia reflect mineralocorticoid failure; hypoglycaemia may result from cortisol deficiency.
Not the most typical: hypercalcaemia can occasionally occur, but is not the characteristic triple compared with hypoglycaemia.

questions.expl: Primary adrenal crisis typically combines hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia from aldosterone deficiency, and sometimes hypoglycaemia from cortisol deficiency. Normal glucose/hypercalcaemia can occur, but other distractor clusters are not most typical.

questions.stem: A local anaesthetic agent that is considered safe to use in a patient with glucose-6- phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is

opts.why: Articaine has been associated with methaemoglobinaemia risk, so it is not the best from these choices.
G6PD deficiency and methemoglobinemia risk; local concentration and dose matter. Avoid drugs associated with methaemoglobinaemia; no medicine is absolutely safe solely because of G6PD deficiency.
Lignocaine can cause methaemoglobinaemia, particularly with high exposure.
Prilocaine metabolite o-toluidine increases methaemoglobinaemia risk.
Benzocaine is strongly associated with acquired methaemoglobinaemia.

questions.expl: Bupivacaine is not a prominent oxidant/methemoglobin former; benzocaine, prilocaine, articaine and sometimes lidocaine have documented methemoglobinemia concern in G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: The ANZAAG-ANZCA guideline for management of resistant hypotension during perioperative refractory anaphylaxis in an adult includes all of the following EXCEPT

questions.stem: The abnormalities seen in the electrocardiogram below are consistent with

opts.why: Hypercalcaemia classically shortens QT rather than creating prominent U waves.
Hypermagnesaemia causes conduction abnormalities but not this characteristic U-wave pattern.
Hyperphosphataemia does not explain the described ECG findings.
Hypokalaemia causes flat T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves.
Hyperkalaemia characteristically produces peaked T waves, later P-wave loss/QRS widening.

questions.expl: The described flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves are the classic ECG constellation of hypokalaemia, especially with loop diuretic losses.

questions.stem: The following supraglottic airway devices allow direct intubation EXCEPT for the

opts.why: Fastrach is designed specifically as an intubating LMA.

opts.why: An i-gel can be used as an intubation conduit with appropriate scope/size technique.

questions.stem: The MELD-Na (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease-Sodium) score includes all of the following parameters EXCEPT

opts.why: Bilirubin is a MELD/MELD-Na variable.
INR is part of MELD.

Creatinine is part of MELD, alongside sodium in MELD-Na.

questions.expl: Conventional MELD-Na uses bilirubin, INR, creatinine and sodium; albumin not included. New 2023 MELD 3.0 does incorporate albumin—explicit scoring system matters. Evidence check: Legacy MELD-Na excludes albumin; MELD 3.0 (in use since 2023) adds it.

questions.stem: Postdural puncture headache in obstetric anaesthesia is associated with a greater likelihood of all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Sheehan stems from postpartum pituitary ischaemia after major haemorrhage. PDPH associations include cerebral venous thrombosis, meningitis and postpartum depression; Sheehan is postpartum pituitary ischaemia.
Cerebral venous thrombosis is an important postpartum headache differential that may coexist with or complicate intracranial hypotension.
Meningitis is a relevant differential/rare complication associated with dural puncture rather than Sheehan syndrome.
Persistent PDPH is associated with postpartum mood symptoms; depression has been reported.

questions.expl: PDPH is associated with cerebral venous thrombosis, meningitis and postpartum depression; Sheehan syndrome instead involves pituitary ischaemia after severe obstetric haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A healthy woman is admitted to the obstetric unit with threatened preterm labour at 29 weeks gestation. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg. A magnesium sulfate infusion is indicated for the purpose of

opts.why: Official Q72 is magnesium neuroprotection. Reconstructed source labels this as #73.
Mild BP elevation without severe hypertension is not the reason to administer magnesium in this threatened-prematurity stem.
There is no diagnosis of severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; prevention of seizures is not the indication.
Magnesium is not recommended solely as a routine tocolytic.

questions.expl: Official Q72 is magnesium neuroprotection. Reconstructed source labels this as #73.

questions.stem: Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors in pregnancy are considered

opts.why: Fetal renal effects and late ductal constriction risk. Official Q73 is COX-2 inhibitors; NSAID fetal renal/ductal risk after mid-pregnancy. Risk is gestational-stage dependent; absolute "unsafe" is simplified.
COX-2/NSAIDs are not safe throughout pregnancy, especially after 20 weeks.
Third-trimester exposure particularly risks ductal constriction and fetal renal effects.

opts.t: Safe from after first trimester until 48h before delivery
opts.why: Risks are not confined to the last 48 h before delivery; fetal renal concerns begin around 20 weeks.

questions.expl: NSAIDs including COX-2 inhibitors can cause fetal renal dysfunction/oligohydramnios after 20 weeks and premature ductal constriction later; neither universally safe nor specifically safe in third trimester.

questions.stem: The commonest symptom or sign of uterine rupture during attempted vaginal birth after caesarean is

opts.why: Pain/tenderness can occur but is less reliably present than fetal heart-rate abnormality.
Commonest objective sign of uterine rupture in TOLAC. Fetal heart-rate abnormality is most common presenting sign of uterine rupture during TOLAC.
Variable decelerations occur but persistent fetal bradycardia is more characteristic in uterine rupture.
Vaginal bleeding is less common and may be concealed.

questions.expl: Persistent fetal bradycardia is a common and clinically important early sign of uterine rupture with VBAC; maternal pain and bleeding may be absent.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old has had a headache for the last month which is relieved by lying flat. They have had no medical procedure to their spine such as epidural, spinal or lumbar puncture. Their brain magnetic resonance (MR) imaging scan shows diffuse meningeal enhancement and brain sagging. The neurologist suspects spontaneous intracranial hypotension and asks you to do an epidural blood patch. No spinal imaging has been performed to confirm a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. You should

opts.t: LP to measure opening pressure then lumbar blood patch if low
opts.why: A lumbar puncture is not required to demonstrate low opening pressure before treating convincing SIH.

opts.t: Non-targeted lumbar EBP without further imaging
opts.why: After initial brain and whole-spine MRI and unsuccessful conservative care, a non-targeted epidural blood patch is an accepted early intervention without invasive leak localisation.

opts.t: Spine imaging then targeted EBP at demonstrated leak
opts.why: Targeted patching ordinarily requires identifying a leak, and is not mandated before a first non-targeted patch.

opts.t: Spine imaging then lumbar EBP only if leak found
opts.why: Absence of visible spinal leakage does not rule out SIH or preclude a non-targeted EBP.
EBP is a recommended first-line intervention for persistent symptomatic SIH after initial conservative care.

questions.expl: The 2023 multidisciplinary SIH consensus recommends brain plus whole-spine MRI as first-line imaging, then early non-targeted epidural blood patch after ineffective conservative measures. A precisely localised leak is not mandatory before a first non-targeted EBP. This rewrites the 2024 stem, which said no spinal imaging had been performed. Evidence check: International consensus: non-targeted EBP before invasive leak localisation in typical SIH

questions.stem: Following scoliosis surgery, a patient exhibits neurological changes in both legs. There is loss of power and reduced pain and temperature sensation. Proprioception and vibration sense are intact. The most likely mechanism of injury is

opts.why: A misplaced screw can cause focal injury but the bilateral motor/pain pattern with preserved dorsal columns is classic anterior-cord vascular syndrome.
Motor and spinothalamic deficits with preserved dorsal-column sensation reflect anterior spinal cord syndrome.
Posterior spinal artery injury would preferentially affect dorsal column modalities.
Brown-Séquard would produce a predominantly hemicord pattern with ipsilateral motor and contralateral pain-temperature loss.

questions.expl: Anterior spinal artery injury causes bilateral motor and pain/temperature loss while dorsal-column vibration and proprioception are relatively preserved.

questions.stem: A seven-year-old child is ventilated in the intensive care unit after an isolated closed head injury. Their serum sodium concentration is 142 mmol/L. The most appropriate intravenous maintenance fluid is

opts.why: 0.45% saline is hypotonic; after brain injury it can worsen sodium reduction and cerebral water accumulation.

opts.t: 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose (isotonic maintenance fluid)
opts.why: Isotonic 0.9% saline with glucose is the routine paediatric maintenance-fluid default here, adjusted to serum sodium and glucose.
5% glucose in water becomes effectively electrolyte-free water after glucose metabolism and is inappropriate for routine maintenance after TBI.
Compound sodium lactate is an isotonic resuscitation fluid, but without glucose is not the preferred maintenance solution for this child; local sodium strategies may differ.
0.3% saline is markedly hypotonic and may aggravate cerebral oedema and hyponatraemia.

questions.expl: Children requiring maintenance fluids generally need isotonic saline with glucose rather than hypotonic fluids; in brain injury, maintain sodium and avoid hypotonic solutions, monitor glucose and electrolytes.

questions.stem: You are anaesthetising an 18-year-old who has a Fontan circulation for exploratory laparotomy. They are intubated and ventilated with a ventilator that has been brought from the Intensive Care Unit. Their current arterial oxygen saturation is 70%. To improve oxygenation, you should INCREASE the

opts.why: Increased peak inspiratory pressure tends to increase intrathoracic pressure and impede passive Fontan pulmonary blood flow.
More PEEP increases mean airway pressure and may reduce Fontan venous return unless there is a separate recruitment indication.
Longer inspiration at a fixed cycle rate shortens expiration and may worsen gas trapping/mean airway pressure.

opts.t: Increase expiratory time to reduce gas trapping and mean airway pressure
opts.why: Documented intrinsic PEEP from incomplete expiration supports lengthening expiration to reduce auto-PEEP and improve venous return.

questions.expl: Fontan physiology favours low peak/mean airway pressure, low PEEP, short inspiratory and longer expiratory time; when flow does not return to baseline, prolonging expiration addresses auto-PEEP.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with a history of asthma is intubated and ventilated for tonsillectomy. During surgery, the SpO2 falls. You increase the FiO2 to 1.0 and hand-ventilate, and note that ventilation is difficult. The next step in the management is to

opts.why: Increasing depth may help bronchospasm, but the temporal association with mouth gag tightening points first to mechanical obstruction.
Salbutamol treats bronchospasm but cannot remove extrinsic ETT compression.

opts.t: Ask the surgeon to release the mouth gag and reassess ETT patency
opts.why: Release the gag promptly and reassess tube position, airway pressure, capnography and ventilation.
Suction may treat secretions but not an obstruction caused by mouth gag tightening; inspect after releasing gag if still impaired.
Further neuromuscular blockade does not relieve gag compression or an angulated tube.

questions.expl: Mouth gags for tonsillectomy can kink, compress or dislodge an ETT; after ventilation worsens immediately following gag tightening, ask the surgeon to release it before attributing obstruction to bronchospasm.

questions.stem: You are called to assist with a patient in the intensive care unit who has had cardiac surgery three days ago and is now in cardiac arrest. External cardiac massage should aim for a systolic blood pressure of

opts.why: 40 mmHg is below the cited compression-generated systolic pressure target.
The post-cardiac-surgery resuscitation target is SBP >60 mmHg when an arterial line is present. The figure is a goal during CPR, not a threshold for starting it.
80 mmHg is higher than the guideline minimum rather than the requested lower threshold.
100 mmHg exceeds the specified minimum.
120 mmHg likewise exceeds the minimum; pressure is only one quality metric.

questions.expl: The post-cardiac-surgery resuscitation target is SBP >60 mmHg when an arterial line is present. The figure is a goal during CPR, not a threshold for starting it. Evidence check: ERC 2025 post-cardiac surgery CPR target SBP >60 mmHg

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting. Immediately upon commencing cardiopulmonary bypass and prior to administering cardioplegia, the aortic line blood appears the same colour as the blood in the venous cannulae, and the low venous saturation alarm is activated on the bypass machine. The most appropriate management at this point is to

opts.t: Reconnect and confirm oxygenator gas supply, checking post-oxygenator oxygenation
opts.why: Re-establish membrane-oxygenator sweep gas/O₂ and confirm oxygenation promptly; persistent severe oxygenator failure needs emergency perfusion/cardiac-team management and potentially circuit change.

opts.t: Increase the blender FiO₂ despite the disconnected supply
opts.why: Increasing blender FiO₂ cannot restore O₂ delivery if the gas supply remains disconnected.

opts.t: Electively wean from bypass before restoring the circuit
opts.why: Coming off bypass without repairing gas failure is dangerous and unnecessary.

opts.t: Continue bypass without correcting the oxygenation fault
opts.why: Continuing hypoxic bypass risks severe systemic oxygen deprivation.
Protamine reverses heparin and does not solve oxygenator gas supply failure.

questions.expl: Dark arterial blood after commencing CPB with disconnected sweep gas requires prompt restoration of oxygenator gas and assessment of post-oxygenator oxygenation.

questions.stem: During rewarming on cardiopulmonary bypass, the most reliable surrogate for cerebral temperature measurement is

opts.why: Nasopharyngeal temperature correlates with brain/core temperature, but STS guidance prefers arterial-outlet blood temperature as cerebral-perfusate surrogate during CPB.

STS/SCA/AmSECT CPB temperature-management guidance (Class I) recommends oxygenator arterial outlet blood temperature as a surrogate for cerebral temperature during CPB. Nasopharyngeal temperature correlates with brain temperature but is recommended principally for core/weaning assessment, not as the preferred cerebral-perfusate surrogate.
Oxygenator venous inlet represents mixed venous/circuit blood rather than cerebral perfusate.
Bladder temperature can lag rapidly changing core/cerebral temperatures during rewarming.
Pulmonary-artery temperature is a reasonable core/weaning monitor but not the Class-I cerebral-perfusate surrogate.

questions.expl: STS/SCA/AmSECT CPB temperature-management guidance (Class I) recommends oxygenator arterial outlet blood temperature as a surrogate for cerebral temperature during CPB. Nasopharyngeal temperature correlates with brain temperature but is recommended principally for core/weaning assessment, not as the preferred cerebral-perfusate surrogate.

questions.stem: The image below is from the transoesophageal echocardiogram of an adult patient who is about to undergo cardiac surgery. The structure labelled with the arrow is the

opts.why: The anterior mitral leaflet is continuous with the mitral–aortic curtain and lies toward the aortic outflow tract.

questions.expl: The 4-hour limit is a maximum, not a requirement that administration take 4 hours. Faster administration can be appropriate. The original 'within' wording leaves shorter answer options technically true.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 22-year-old man is involved in an altercation and sustains a ruptured spleen. During splenectomy he is transfused with packed red blood cells. One hour into the transfusion his SpO2 rapidly decreases, his ventilator pressures increase, frothy sputum appears in the endotracheal tube and he is febrile. The likely cause is

opts.why: TRALI is new noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema during/within 6 h transfusion in absence of left-atrial hypertension. TACO instead has volume-overload features.
TACO usually has hydrostatic overload evidence (raised pressure/JVP, positive fluid balance, cardiac dysfunction).
Delayed haemolytic reaction typically occurs days later and presents with haemolysis, not acute isolated noncardiogenic oedema.
Mild allergic urticaria does not explain bilateral pulmonary infiltrates/hypoxaemia.
Post-transfusion purpura is a delayed thrombocytopenic syndrome, not acute respiratory failure.

questions.expl: TRALI presents as hypoxaemic, bilateral noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6h of transfusion; differentiate from TACO with volume overload/cardiac dysfunction.

questions.stem: The main difference between a size 5 microlaryngeal tube (MLT) and a standard size 5 endotracheal tube is that the size 5 MLT

opts.why: An MLT is not defined by having a shorter shaft than an ordinary size-5 tube.

opts.t: A longer tube length despite the small internal diameter
opts.why: Device manufacturers confirm a size 5 microlaryngeal tube has a 5mm internal diameter but adult-length shaft; the Sher idan LTS product is 321mm long with an adult-sized cuff. This is not a uniquely different ID or connector.
Cuff dimensions differ by manufacturer, but simply 'larger cuff diameter' is not the defining universal contrast.
A standard breathing-circuit connector is used; a unique sampling connector is not its main feature.

questions.expl: Microlaryngeal ETT has a small internal diameter but longer tube body appropriate for adult surgical access; standard 5.0 tube may be short.

questions.stem: When using an endotracheal tube in an adult, the highest recommended cuff pressure to avoid mucosal ischaemia is

opts.why: 10 cmH₂O often risks inadequate cuff sealing/aspiration protection rather than being the recommended maximum.
20 cmH₂O is within the target range, but not the usual upper recommended limit.
Recommended ETT cuff pressure range 20–30cmH₂O to reduce tracheal mucosal ischaemia.
40 cmH₂O exceeds the mucosal-pressure safety target.
50 cmH₂O is substantially above the recommended limit.

questions.expl: 20–30 cm H2O is common ETT cuff target, with 30 an upper bound, though prolonged pressures at the top of the range can still cause mucosal injury.

questions.stem: The sensor on a NIM (Nerve Integrity Monitor) endotracheal tube used for thyroid surgery directly records

opts.why: Surface electrodes on NIM tube record activity from vocalis/thyroarytenoid muscles.
The NIM tube detects laryngeal-muscle EMG via surface electrodes; it does not directly record nerve action potentials.
Cuff pressure is not the electrically measured signal.
The tube does not use an optical motion sensor.
Tracheal temperature is not the NIM monitoring target.

questions.expl: Surface electrodes on NIM tube record activity from vocalis/thyroarytenoid muscles. Evidence check: NIM ETT surface electrodes record vocalis muscle EMG, not RLN nerve action potentials

questions.stem: Double sequential external defibrillation is performed by applying two shocks from

opts.why: One set of pads cannot deliver the two distinct sequential shocks/orthogonal vectors described.
One pad set remains the wrong configuration regardless of interval.
The DOSE VF DSED protocol uses two separate pad sets and shocks in rapid succession, with <1 s delay.
A deliberate delay of 3–5 s between shocks is not the rapid-sequence (<1 s) interval specified in the DOSE VF protocol.
Simultaneous rather than rapidly sequential shocks do not match the specified protocol.

questions.expl: DOSE VF employed two separate defibrillators and two sets of pads in alternate vectors, with rapid sequential (approximately <1 s) shocks. ANZCOR notes that routine DSED is not established outside selected refractory VF circumstances. Specify the trial protocol for an exact interval. Evidence check: DOSE VF protocol: two pad pairs, shocks <1 s apart sequentially, not simultaneous; does not imply routine clinical endorsement

questions.stem: The initial management for a seizure during an awake craniotomy is

opts.why: First-response step for seizure during awake mapping is chilled saline to cortex; persistent seizure -> sedative medication.
Propofol can abort persistent intraoperative seizures, but local cold-saline irrigation is the immediate first manoeuvre for stimulation-induced awake-craniotomy seizure.
Releasing pins does not terminate a cortical stimulus-induced seizure.
Carbamazepine is not a rapid IV abortive treatment.
Intubation/hyperventilation may be required for prolonged seizures/airway compromise, not the initial routine action.

questions.expl: Seizure at awake craniotomy with cortical stimulation: stop stimulus and promptly irrigate exposed cortex with ice-cold saline; give IV anticonvulsant if persistent.

questions.stem: A new antiemetic reduces the risk of post-operative vomiting by 20%. In a population with a baseline risk of post-operative vomiting of 10%, the number needed to treat is

opts.why: NNT 2 would imply a 50% absolute risk reduction, impossible with a 10% baseline event risk.
NNT 5 implies 20 percentage-point absolute reduction, not 20% relative reduction.
NNT 10 implies 10 percentage-point absolute reduction.
NNT 20 implies a 5-point absolute reduction, larger than the calculated 2-point reduction.
A 20% relative reduction from baseline 10% means event risk 8%, absolute benefit 2 percentage points, NNT 1/0.02 = 50.

questions.expl: Control risk 10%; relative risk reduction 20%; treated risk 8%; absolute risk reduction 2 percentage points = 0.02; NNT=1/0.02=50. If the stem instead meant a 20-percentage-point absolute reduction, the data would be inconsistent.

questions.stem: A risk factor which increases the likelihood of developing local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is

opts.why: Hypoxaemia and acidosis aggravate LAST; high protein binding lowers unbound fraction.
Alkalemia generally decreases local-anaesthetic toxicity risk relative to acidosis, though it changes non-ionised fraction.
More α1-acid glycoprotein increases binding and reduces free drug concentration.
Hypocarbia is not the classic risk state; hypercarbia/acidosis potentiates LAST.
Carnitine status is not an established routine risk factor in this option set.

questions.expl: Hypoxia/acidosis can worsen local anaesthetic systemic toxicity by affecting tissue uptake and cardiac/cerebral sensitivity; options suggesting reduced risk are wrong.

opts.t: Non-inferiority is established, but superiority is not established because the CI includes 0
opts.why: The entire CI is below the prespecified harm margin (+10%), establishing NI, but it spans 0 so superiority is not demonstrated. This is a newly authored numeric example, not the missing trial M plot.

opts.t: Non-inferiority fails because the confidence interval touches 0
opts.why: Crossing zero is not the criterion for noninferiority; the upper bound versus +10% margin is.
