opts.why: The CI spans zero, so benefit/superiority is not demonstrated.

opts.t: No conclusion is possible without sample size
opts.why: The prespecified margin and CI are sufficient for the stated noninferiority conclusion, conditional on valid trial conduct.

questions.expl: Noninferiority margin is upper +10% for an undesirable outcome; 95%CI −18% to +2% lies below +10% but spans zero: noninferiority proven, superiority not proven.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old athlete undergoing a knee arthroscopy under general anaesthesia develops intraoperative tachycardia. A 12-lead electrocardiogram is obtained and shown below. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: AF is irregular unless unusually organised and does not explain a regular 1:1 AV re-entrant rhythm.
Flutter often shows flutter waves and different AV conduction and is not the classic accessory-pathway orthodromic mechanism.
Sinus tachycardia has a sinoatrial activation pattern, not retrograde eccentric P waves.
Antegrade conduction via AV node and retrograde conduction via accessory pathway produces orthodromic AVRT. A 12-lead ECG alone may not always distinguish this from AVNRT without further information.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with multiple P morphologies.

questions.expl: Orthodromic AV re-entry travels antegrade through AV node and retrograde via accessory pathway, usually narrow complex; antidromic typically broad.

questions.stem: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a statistical test to determine

opts.t: Goodness of fit observed vs expected
opts.why: Chi-square goodness-of-fit typically compares observed and expected frequencies.
ANOVA tests between-group variation in means relative to within-group variation.
A two-group nonparametric comparison uses tests such as Mann–Whitney, not ANOVA.
Comparing medians/distributions across groups may use Kruskal–Wallis, not a standard parametric ANOVA.
ANOVA assumes certain variance properties; it is not a test for normality.

questions.expl: ANOVA compares means across groups by between-group versus within-group variation, not categorical proportions or simple individual correlations.

questions.stem: When performing a brachial plexus block at the level of the axilla, the structure indicated by the arrow is the

opts.why: The musculocutaneous nerve usually lies separately between biceps and coracobrachialis, not as the classic anterolateral perivascular nerve.
Radial nerve typically has a more posteromedial/posterior relationship to the artery.
Ulnar nerve is usually medial to the artery rather than anterolateral.
Correct for the classic arrangement: median nerve is commonly anterolateral to the axillary artery, though real-world position varies.
Axillary nerve is not routinely seen adjacent to the axillary artery at the level used for the distal axillary plexus block.

questions.expl: Median nerve is commonly anterolateral to axillary artery in classic axillary sonographic view, with important inter-individual variability.

questions.stem: A third heart sound at the apex may be heard in

opts.why: An S3 can be physiological in children, younger adults and pregnancy; in a middle-aged/older adult it is more concerning for volume overload or impaired LV function. The new choices are educational rather than source-recovered.
Uncomplicated MVP may create clicks/murmurs, but isolated MVP does not characteristically cause an S3.
Hypertension without ventricular failure does not typically produce a physiologic S3.
First-degree AV block affects conduction and is not a source of early diastolic filling sound.
Mild isolated AS is not a classic cause of S3 unless significant dysfunction coexists.

questions.expl: Physiological third heart sounds occur in some younger healthy individuals; older adults with heart failure may also have pathological S3.

questions.stem: In pulmonary function testing the presence of airflow limitation is defined by a post- bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio less than

opts.why: FEV1/FVC <0.50 represents more pronounced obstruction, not the GOLD threshold.
<0.60 is also below the recommended fixed diagnostic cutoff.
Under GOLD, post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 is the specific cutoff for persistent obstructive physiology in COPD.
<0.80 is too high for the fixed GOLD obstruction criterion, especially in adults; LLN interpretation also matters.

questions.expl: GOLD specifies a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 for COPD diagnosis in the right clinical context; age-related LLN differences remain relevant in borderline patients.

questions.stem: Local anaesthetic-induced myotoxicity is most likely to be associated with

opts.why: Local anaesthetics, notably bupivacaine, can produce dose- and exposure-related skeletal-muscle myotoxicity following intramuscular administration; symptoms and risk depend on site/dose/duration.

opts.t: Injection of isotonic saline around a peripheral nerve
opts.why: Normal saline around a nerve does not have local-anaesthetic skeletal myocyte toxicity.

opts.t: Systemic lidocaine infusion with no tissue infiltration
opts.why: Systemic IV lidocaine does not give the same high local intramuscular exposure.
Preservative-free saline is not intrinsically myotoxic in the same fashion.

opts.t: Local anaesthetic remaining entirely within a vascular compartment
opts.why: Purely intravascular LA exposure may be systemically toxic but not direct local skeletal-muscle myotoxicity.

questions.expl: Direct intramuscular exposure to bupivacaine is linked to dose-dependent reversible local myotoxicity, unlike oral paracetamol or topical nonspecific therapies.

questions.stem: Regarding healthcare research, the PICO framework describes

opts.t: Formulation of a clinical research question using Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome
opts.why: PICO structures clinical questions for evidence appraisal and literature searches.

opts.t: A statistical technique for a meta-analysis
opts.why: PICO guides question formulation, rather than directly performing statistical pooling.

opts.t: A randomisation method for an RCT
opts.why: Randomisation is an allocation process and not what PICO denotes.
PICO applies to many clinical research questions, not only one diagnostic-study design.

questions.expl: PICO = Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome; it formulates answerable clinical questions rather than selecting a p value or trial randomisation.

questions.stem: The 12-lead electrocardiogram shown is most consistent with acute total occlusion of the

opts.why: Anterior/septal leads V1–V4 map most strongly to LAD. I and aVL reflect high lateral extension and anatomy can vary; original ECG not provided.
PDA typically supplies the inferior/posterior walls rather than anterior precordial ST elevation.
A solitary obtuse marginal lesion more commonly produces lateral patterns without the classic anterior V2–V4 changes.
RCA typically produces inferior ST elevation or posterior changes.
SA nodal artery occlusion is not the usual cause of widespread anterior STEMI.

questions.expl: In a practice ECG explicitly describing V2–V4 with I/aVL ST elevation, anterolateral STEMI suggests LAD culprit; original image still required to authenticate original.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient booked for a revision total hip replacement is reviewed in preadmission clinic ten days before surgery. The following blood test results are noted: haemoglobin 110 g/L; ferritin 51 mcg/L; CRP (c-reactive protein) 10 mg/L. The most appropriate management for this patient should be to

opts.why: At Hb 110 g/L without instability, two units RBC are not routine first-line treatment for iron-deficiency anaemia.
Oral iron may work over weeks, but 10 days is a short window for a reliable meaningful response.
Delaying major surgery for several weeks might be appropriate in an elective case after MDT discussion, but is not the immediate iron-repletion method among listed options.
Low transferrin saturation plus ferritin 51 with inflammation supports iron deficiency, and IV iron offers faster repletion with only 10 days available.
Untreated anaemia/iron deficiency raises perioperative risk; assessment and management are indicated.

questions.expl: Anaemia with ferritin 51 in inflammation and TSAT <20% supports iron deficiency; at ten days to major surgery, IV iron is reasonable versus slowly acting oral iron. Alternatives depend on clinical urgency.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with no past history of ischaemic heart disease is three days post- total hip replacement surgery. They have an episode of chest pain at rest with features typical of angina that lasts 30 minutes before fully resolving. There are no electrocardiogram changes and no troponin rise. The diagnosis is

opts.why: Resting typical ischaemic pain merits assessment for unstable angina even with no biomarker elevation.
Rest angina without troponin rise/ECG ST elevation is consistent with unstable angina; must rule out alternate causes.
STEMI requires characteristic ST-segment elevation/equivalent.
NSTEMI requires an acute rise/fall in troponin with ischaemia.
MINS is defined by postoperative troponin elevation attributable to ischaemia; none is present.

questions.expl: Rest angina without troponin rise/ECG ST elevation is consistent with unstable angina; must rule out alternate causes. Evidence check: Rest pain with no troponin rise/ECG changes may be unstable angina after appropriate assessment; clinical differentiation from noncardiac pain is needed

questions.stem: The QRS axis of the attached electrocardiograph is closest to

opts.why: −90° is a more extreme left axis; a positive lead I and negative lead II fits an axis left of −30°, commonly around −45°.
Positive I, negative aVF indicates leftward axis, and negative lead II puts the axis below approximately −30 degrees, so −45 degrees is the best of these choices. Actual ECG not supplied.
+45° should produce positive lead II.
+90° generally produces negative or isoelectric lead I, positive aVF.
+150° generally produces negative lead I and positive inferior leads.

questions.expl: QRS I positive, II negative and aVF negative corresponds to left axis deviation below −30°, with −45° among the given choices.

questions.stem: In septic shock, the recommended target mean arterial pressure in an adult is

opts.why: 50 mmHg is below the standard initial adult septic shock MAP target.
55 mmHg is below the usual minimum.
60 mmHg is below the guideline's DEFAULT target for 18–64-year-olds; SSC 2026 separately suggests 60–65 mmHg for adults >=65.
SSC default initial MAP target for adults with septic shock remains 65mmHg with individualized targets.

questions.expl: The SSC 2026 guideline recommends an initial MAP target of 65 mmHg for adults. It separately suggests 60–65 mmHg in those aged 65 years or older; the stem specifies a younger adult to eliminate this caveat.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with carcinoid syndrome undergoing resection of a peripheral hepatic metastasis develops a sudden fall in blood pressure from 110/70 mmHg to 85/50 mmHg without significant bleeding. The most appropriate management is

opts.t: IV vasopressors (e.g. phenylephrine/noradrenaline), with octreotide as adjunct as needed
opts.why: A 2026 international consensus now favours vasopressors for haemodynamic instability and octreotide as an adjunct. Historical octreotide-first language is not the best current answer.

opts.t: Octreotide as sole primary haemodynamic treatment while withholding pressors
opts.why: Withholding pressors in profound hypotension conflicts with current haemodynamic resuscitation guidance.

opts.t: IV calcium as the sole therapy
opts.why: Calcium alone does not treat the vasodilatory/mediator component of crisis.
Observation is inappropriate in profound haemodynamic compromise.
Empirical heparin does not reverse carcinoid mediator-induced crisis.

questions.expl: A 2026 international consensus now favours vasopressors for haemodynamic instability and octreotide as an adjunct. Historical octreotide-first language is not the best current answer. Evidence check: Oct 2026 expert consensus: pressors first-line; octreotide adjunct when needed

questions.stem: In cardiac surgery a low-normal central venous pressure and a low blood pressure with a hyperdynamic heart is suggestive of

opts.why: Preserved/increased cardiac output with low SVR supports vasoplegia. Hypotension with a hyperdynamic LV and low CVP ALONE cannot distinguish vasoplegia from hypovolaemia.

opts.t: Isolated hypovolaemia with proven fluid responsiveness
opts.why: Proven isolated volume depletion/positive fluid responsiveness is contradicted by adequate filling and measured low SVR; actual responsiveness needs testing.
Low-output cardiogenic shock conflicts with a normal cardiac output and hyperdynamic LV.
Tamponade requires characteristic filling limitation/obstructive findings, not simply low SVR.
Massive PE is obstructive with RV strain/reduced forward flow, not isolated normal-output low-SVR vasoplegia.

questions.expl: Measured low SVR with normal output, adequate filling and hypotension indicates vasoplegia, unlike low-output cardiogenic shock, tamponade, PE or proven hypovolaemia.

questions.stem: One metabolic equivalent (1MET) is defined as the

opts.why: Walking at 4 km/h requires greater than resting metabolic energy expenditure and is multiple METs.
Conventionally one MET is resting oxygen consumption, approximately 3.5 mL/kg/min in an average adult.
Walking at 4 km/h requires more energy than rest, so it does not define one MET.

opts.t: Oxygen consumption during brisk uphill walking
opts.why: Brisk uphill walking requires far more oxygen than rest and therefore exceeds one MET.

questions.expl: A conventional adult metabolic equivalent is resting oxygen uptake ~3.5 mL/kg/min. Walking demands more than one MET.

questions.stem: According to the Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation guidelines, the minimum distance a defibrillation pad should be placed away from a pacemaker or implantable cardiac defibrillator generator is

opts.why: 4 cm is closer to the generator than the cited ≥8-cm separation.
ANZCOR recommends defibrillation pads at least ~8cm from implanted generator where practicable.
12 cm satisfies 'at least 8 cm' but is NOT the specified MINIMUM ideal separation quoted by ANZCOR (8 cm).
16 cm exceeds the minimum; it is not the guideline's named ideal minimum 8 cm.
20 cm exceeds the minimum; it is not the guideline's named ideal minimum 8 cm.

questions.expl: ANZCOR recommends placing defibrillation pads ideally at least 8 cm away from the generator, without delaying shock delivery. A separation greater than 8 cm is also acceptable; 8 cm is the guideline's named ideal minimum.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old sustains a burn to 30% of their total body surface area. A physiological change expected within the first 24 hours is

opts.why: Early major burn shock usually decreases cardiac index before the later hyperdynamic phase.
Early burn shock is associated with vasoconstriction/high SVR, not typical reduced SVR.
Immediately after severe burn, low cardiac output and high vascular resistance. Acute major burn ebb response has low cardiac output and elevated vascular resistance; later flow phase reverses.
Splanchnic/hepatic flow usually falls during early hypovolaemic burn shock.

questions.expl: Published acute burn physiology review demonstrates low cardiac output and elevated systemic AND pulmonary vascular resistance in the first 24–48 hours, prior to the later hyperdynamic period.

questions.stem: When inadvertent total spinal anaesthesia occurs in an awake neonate, the first sign is most likely to be

opts.t: Apnoea or marked loss of respiratory effort
opts.why: Respiratory arrest/apnoea can be the first clinically apparent indicator of high neuraxial blockade in neonates; desaturation may be a subsequent finding.
High neuraxial block usually causes hypotension/bradycardia, not sustained hypertension.
Tachypnoea with preserved effort is less characteristic than progressive respiratory depression/apnoea.
Hyperreflexia is not the expected early high-block sign.
Hyperthermia is not a characteristic consequence of sudden high spinal.

questions.expl: Excessively high neuraxial spread in neonates may cause respiratory muscle impairment and apnoea, unlike isolated expected low-segment analgesia.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has ROTEM results including: [table attached]. The most appropriate treatment is

opts.why: Platelet replacement alone will not correct very low FIBTEM fibrin-based clot strength.
Marked FIBTEM amplitude reduction indicates reduced fibrin-based clot strength and supports fibrinogen replacement. Actual transfusion should follow local ROTEM algorithms and clinical bleeding.
Protamine is indicated for residual heparin, not low fibrinogen amplitude when heparin is not implicated.
TXA treats hyperfibrinolysis, not isolated profound fibrinogen deficiency.
Active bleeding plus FIBTEM A5 3 mm warrants targeted haemostatic management, not observation.

questions.expl: Very low FIBTEM A5 demonstrates inadequate fibrin contribution so fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate is the first ROTEM-directed correction, not platelets in isolation.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old has a laryngeal mask airway inserted for a surgical procedure. The following day it is noted that the tongue is deviated to the right. The most likely site of nerve injury is the right

opts.why: Glossopharyngeal injury causes posterior tongue/pharyngeal sensory and taste dysfunction, not ipsilateral protrusion weakness.
Lingual nerve injury causes anterior tongue sensory/taste changes, not motor deviation.
Facial nerve injury may affect taste/facial motor function, not tongue protrusion.
Vagus nerve affects palate/larynx rather than genioglossus protrusion.
Ipsilateral hypoglossal lower motor neuron lesion produces tongue deviation to affected side.

questions.expl: Hypoglossal nerve palsy after airway instrumentation produces ipsilateral tongue weakness and deviation toward side of injury; glossopharyngeal/vagus lesions produce different signs.

questions.stem: The nerve marked by the arrow is the

opts.why: Axillary nerve innervates deltoid/teres minor and passes quadrangular space, not suprascapular notch.
Radial nerve supplies posterior arm/forearm extensors.
The suprascapular nerve passes under the transverse scapular ligament at the suprascapular notch, then supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
Musculocutaneous supplies anterior arm muscles.
Long thoracic supplies serratus anterior on lateral chest wall.

questions.expl: Suprascapular nerve passes beneath superior transverse scapular ligament at suprascapular notch, in contrast to suprascapular artery (typically above).

questions.stem: In an adult weighing 70 kg, a bedside assessment of haemodynamic status shows a left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 2.4 cm. This finding suggests

opts.t: A small LV cavity compatible with reduced filling, which alone does NOT prove fluid responsiveness
opts.why: A small LV can reflect underfilling or small chamber size, but a static LV diameter cannot confirm absolute volume status or responsiveness to a fluid bolus.
A single small LV dimension cannot prove normal preload.
A small end-diastolic diameter does not establish hypervolaemia.

opts.t: Severe chronic LV dilatation is present
opts.why: A 2.4-cm cavity is small, not severely dilated.
LV cavity dimension alone does not diagnose pulmonary hypertension; RV and pulmonary haemodynamics are needed.

questions.expl: LV end-diastolic internal diameter 2.4 cm indicates a small cavity but alone does not prove fluid responsiveness without clinical and dynamic haemodynamic measures.

questions.stem: For driving pressure guided ventilation, driving pressure is the

opts.why: For a passive ventilator patient, driving pressure = plateau airway pressure − total PEEP; equivalently, it equals tidal volume divided by measured static respiratory-system compliance. The previously authored option 'VT divided by compliance' was ALSO correct, so this practice version replaces it with an explicitly incorrect 'VT multiplied by compliance' distractor.

opts.t: Peak airway pressure minus total PEEP
opts.why: Peak pressure includes resistive pressure components, so peak−PEEP overestimates elastic driving pressure.
Mean airway pressure is an averaged ventilation-cycle quantity, not driving pressure.

opts.t: Plateau pressure minus peak airway pressure
opts.why: Plateau−peak represents a pressure related to resistance (with reversed sign), not ΔP.

opts.t: Tidal volume multiplied by static respiratory-system compliance
opts.why: Multiplying tidal volume by static compliance gives incorrect units and relationship; note that VT DIVIDED BY static compliance would be mathematically equivalent to the correct answer.

questions.expl: For a passive ventilator patient, driving pressure = plateau airway pressure − total PEEP; equivalently, it equals tidal volume divided by measured static respiratory-system compliance. The previously authored option 'VT divided by compliance' was ALSO correct, so this practice version replaces it with an explicitly incorrect 'VT multiplied by compliance' distractor.
